title: The Pharmacist Who Invented Birth Control
event_summary: Mexican chemist Luis Miramontes, a 26-year-old research assistant working under Carl Djerassi and George Rosenkranz at Laboratorios Syntex, synthesized norethindrone — the first orally active progestational compound — from barbasco root yams harvested by Indigenous farmers in Veracruz. This single molecule became the active ingredient in the first oral contraceptive pill. Miramontes performed the critical synthesis that neither Djerassi nor Rosenkranz had achieved, yet his notebook entry from that day would be largely erased from popular history.
why_forgotten: Credit was overwhelmingly directed to Djerassi, an Austrian-American émigré who became known as the 'father of the pill,' while Miramontes — a young Mexican national — was sidelined in English-language histories shaped by Cold War cultural hierarchies. Mexico's own pharmaceutical industry was later gutted by multinational consolidation, erasing the memory that a Latin American laboratory had produced one of the century's most consequential inventions. The Indigenous knowledge of barbasco yam's hormonal properties, which made the synthesis economically viable, was never credited at all.
why_it_matters: Norethindrone enabled the oral contraceptive pill approved in 1960, which reshaped global demographics, women's workforce participation, and family structures in ways still unfolding today. The episode also established the template for bioprospecting controversies — extracting Indigenous botanical knowledge for corporate profit — that remains central to debates over genetic resources and intellectual property. Mexico City's forgotten role as a birthplace of reproductive technology challenges persistent assumptions about where transformative science originates.
